solver.kind: blind AI solver (separate agent, answer-free packet, rubric v2)

R055-01.notes: Arc: transcription builds the language (para 3), then the forgotten-phrase night makes it 'mine' (para 4), and the close says the lesson 'runs both ways'. B reduces improvisation to memorized material; the passage says that stage said 'nothing in particular'. C contradicts 'He was right' and the fact that the narrator still assigns transcriptions. D: nothing compares jazz with other music, and the passage stresses jazz's rules.

R055-02.notes: Para 2 explains it: improvisers work within chords, while the narrator played 'whatever came into my head'. A: volume is never at issue. B: the conversation analogy says improvisers have 'not rehearsed', so planning every note is wrong. D: copying the recording is the opposite of improvising.

R055-03.notes: 'Speakers have not rehearsed their words, yet they share a language whose rules...' = unrehearsed but rule-governed. A contradicts 'not rehearsed'. C: clashing is mentioned in the previous sentence, but it is not the purpose of the analogy. D is absurdly literal.

R055-04.notes: Para 3 says this nearly verbatim: 'listen to a recording..., slow it down, and write out every note by ear.' A: it was done by ear, not from sheet music. B: playing along is the first lesson, not transcription. C: inventing is the opposite of copying.

R055-05.notes: The preceding clause says 'a voice is built from what it has absorbed'. B: he treats a voice as the goal, built through absorption; he does not tell students to give it up. C: no difficulty comparison. D: copying is the means, not the 'final goal'.

R055-06.notes: The next sentences: imitations only, 'collages of borrowed phrases... saying nothing', and the breakthrough 'was not a matter of learning more'. A: the narrator still assigns transcriptions. C: the voice came after the transcribing, not before. D: nothing is said about how great saxophonists learned.

R055-07.notes: 'Collages of borrowed phrases, stitched together.' A is the literal art sense, a standard trap. B contradicts 'half a dozen musicians' and 'stitched together'. D: no summarizing is involved.

R055-08.notes: 'Had to find my own way back to the chord... It was also... mine.' A contradicts 'What I played was clumsy.' B: no praise from Okafor is mentioned. C: no timeline for stopping transcription is given, and the narrator still values it.

R055-09.notes: 'Without the occasional mistake that forces you off the script, there is no one saying it' = personal expression needs departure from learned material. A overstates: 'occasional', not 'as many as possible'. C contradicts 'I still assign transcriptions.' D is the reverse of the sentence's emphasis, and the passage says both are needed.

R055-10.notes: 'I still assign transcriptions. But I also tell my students about that night' and 'Without the language, there is nothing to say.' A: 'only reliable way' is too strong, since the narrator adds the lesson of that night. B: 'He was right' and the narrator still assigns it. D: the narrator does not doubt its value.

flags.note: Passage A never literally says 'every city'. The key rests on A's general claim that code numbers are not how parking 'ought to be decided', which is fair but slightly inferential. Also, B is the only option that is a proposal; A, C and D are factual statements Passage B never disputes. Paired with the stem word 'proposal', that partly gives the key away without reading.

R055-11.notes: Passage B's final sentence: 'Eliminating minimums everywhere at once trades one uniform rule for another.' This targets A's endorsement of eliminating minimums as a general policy. A: B does not dispute the cost. C: B does not address the original purpose. D: B does not deny that cities eliminated minimums.
